lead.en: When the lights and noise of a military lorry reached a night column of 260 horses from Janów Podlaski in September 1939, eighty of them bolted. The young stallion Witeź was led back and recognised by the crowned J branded on his shoulder. A crowned J also stands on the stud's gate today.

paragraphs.en: The 2017 sheetlet marks 200 years of the stud at Janów Podlaski. Each of its nine stamps shows an Arabian horse at a white paddock fence and names it in capitals, PINGA and PIANISSIMA among them. With the sheetlet on the desk, the question is where this stud is and what of its history can still be seen there.

paragraphs.en: Opened again from the collection, the stamp now carries the badge "In Collection". "Show on map" moves to its pin at Janów Podlaski, north of Biała Podlaska in the east of Poland. Twenty stamps from 1963 to 2017 share this pin. Paging through them leads to a stallion on a stamp of 1967 that reads "JANÓW PODLASKI 1817-1967". The pin sits in the village. The stud is in Wygoda, about 2 km to the north-east.

paragraphs.en: German planes attacked the stud on 4 September 1939. The next day the horses and 19 wagons left Janów in a column two kilometres long, moving only at night. One night the lights and noise of a military lorry made the horses bolt. Eighty of them ran off, the young stallion Witeź among them.

paragraphs.en: Witeź stayed at Janów until 1942. That year he was taken to Młynów in Volhynia and then to Hostau in the Sudetes. On 28 April 1945 the horses of Hostau were moved 300 km to Bavaria, with Witeź ridden for part of the way. A ship took him on to the US Army remount station at Front Royal, Virginia. He died on a pasture in 1965.

paragraphs.en: A path through the park leads to the horse cemetery, where granite boulders carry bronze plaques for horses that served the stud. Two of the names are on the 2017 sheetlet. One plaque reads "PIANISSIMA / Gazal Al Shaqab - Pianosa / 2003 - 2015", another "PINGA / Gazal Al Shaqab - Pilar / 2004-2021". Pianissima died in October 2015, two years before her stamp was issued. Pinga died in Minnesota at the end of March 2021.

paragraphs.en: The map has a pin at Kodeń, on the Bug about 40 km south-east of the stud. Kodeń is reached by car. The sanctuary's own account tells that Mikołaj Sapieha fell ill in 1629 while building his church there. He travelled to Rome and was healed at a Mass of Pope Urban VIII in front of an image of the Virgin. The pope refused to give it to him. By the same account, Sapieha promised the papal sacristan 500 gold ducats for it and reached Kodeń with the image on 15 September 1631.
